subject: baz — the Vibe playlist page, next phase
reason: The owner reviewed the contour page shipped in 0.2.0 and the redesign proposed in docs/design/19-vibe-next-phase.md, and said it 'still feels like it hasn't addressed everything'. This room exists to find what the proposal missed.
reading: docs/design/impl/vibe-next-phase/ — the page photographed at 1600x900 and 1000x700
docs/design/16-local-vibe-playlists.md — what the engine actually does
docs/design/impl/contour/ — the contour as built, with its own frames
docs/design/impl/vibe-memory/ — what a compose costs in memory

participants.name: Ines Aro
participants.note: Twenty years of shipping player software; wrote components for foobar2000. Speaks for the listener with 40,000 files.

participants.name: Marcus Tey
participants.note: Audio embeddings and text-audio retrieval. Knows exactly what a CLAP text tower will and will not answer.

participants.name: Priya Raghavan
participants.note: Direct manipulation; automation lanes and curve editors in production audio tools.

participants.name: Jonas Feld
participants.note: Labels, microcopy and mental models. Argues that words are the interface.

participants.name: Wren Oyelaran
participants.note: WCAG, colour vision, keyboard and motor access. Holds the product to its own published promises.

participants.name: Sam Boateng
participants.note: Cuts options. In the room because the owner said an expert would say 'don't give them all these options'.

participants.name: Lena Fischer
participants.note: What the analysis costs in time, memory and battery, and what that does to the first run.

participants.name: Toby Hall
participants.note: Nine thousand tracks, no interest in how any of it works. The proxy for the person the page is for.

participants.name: facilitator
participants.note: Seeds the questions, keeps score, and owns the resolutions.

text: Thank you all for coming. On the table: baz composes a playlist from your own music, locally, with no language model and no network. The page that does it shipped a fortnight ago and the owner's verdict is that the layout is wrong and the whole thing is uninviting. I proposed a two-pane redesign — controls left, list right — and his response was that it still hasn't addressed everything. So: find what it hasn't. Start wherever you like.

The two-pane call is right and it's also the least interesting thing in the document. Every player that composes anything shows you the result beside the controls. What I want to know is what happens on the second Tuesday, when the listener has already made four of these and wants a fifth in ten seconds.

Can I say the obvious thing first? I opened it and I didn't know what I was supposed to type. It says describe the music you want. I typed 'stuff for driving at night' and got a playlist that had a live orchestral record in it.

That's not a bug, and it's the single most important thing in this room. The text tower is a CLAP-family model. It was trained on audio and captions — 'a recording of a solo piano, soft and melancholic'. It answers descriptions of *sound*. 'Stuff for driving at night' is a description of an *occasion*, and the model has almost nothing to hang that on, so you get whatever the nearest neighbours in embedding space happen to be. Which can be an orchestra.
So the box is lying to me.
The box is under-specified. The proposal's line — 'describe the sound, not the story' — is correct and it is not enough, because it tells you what not to do without giving you a route.

This is my whole objection to the redesign as drawn. It has a rule and two example chips. A rule without a route is a scold. If the model wants timbre, instruments and moods, then give people timbre, instruments and moods — a small vocabulary they can build a phrase out of, in three rows: what it's made of, what it feels like, how it moves. Chips that append to the field. Typing stays possible for the people who know what they're doing.

Build-a-phrase rather than fill-a-box. That also fixes the affordance complaint underneath it: a row of chips that visibly changes the text in the field teaches you what kind of words go there in about four seconds.
I'll allow it if the vocabulary is small. Three rows of six is eighteen chips and that's a menu. Three rows of four, chosen because they're the axes the model actually resolves, is a vocabulary.

Twelve is defensible. I'd want the words chosen against the baseline corpus rather than by taste — there's already a scoring harness in the tree for exactly this, `vibe-baseline`. Pick the chips that measurably retrieve, not the ones that read nicely.
Noted, and that's item 59 in the backlog — how the engine is prompted, unstarted, and it says no prompt change ships without a scored run. This would be its first customer.

I want to interrupt the words conversation with the thing that outranks it. The proposal says a mood press composes immediately. On a library that has never been analysed, that sentence is false. Baz has to listen to every track before it can place any of them, and that is minutes to hours, not milliseconds.

The numbers we actually have: a 24-track fixture completes inside a 90-second sampling window at four workers, and each worker costs about 145 MiB of runtime arena. Nobody has measured a per-track rate on a real library, so I won't invent one — but order of magnitude, a nine-thousand-track library is hours of CPU. The page cannot open with a control that promises a playlist in one press.
It did say something about nothing analysed yet. I didn't know what that meant so I ignored it and pressed the button.
Of course you did. There was a button, so you pressed it.
So the cold start is the design and the proposal treats it as a footnote. That's the first real miss. Priya, what does the first run look like?

It looks like the page's main state, not an error state. When the library is unlistened, the right-hand pane isn't an empty list — it's the progress, in the listener's terms, with a partial result appearing in it as tracks land. 'Baz has listened to 240 of your 9,412 tracks. You can leave this page; it keeps going.' And the mood chips stay pressable, because pressing one is a perfectly good way to say what to work towards.
And the progress has to be a real reading, not a spinner. A spinner on an hours-long job is a lie told sixty times a second.

There's a second-order question the proposal never asks: may baz start listening *before* somebody visits this page? On first launch, quietly, in the background? That is hours of CPU and, on a laptop, battery. It is a consent question and it belongs to the owner, not to us.
Strong agree it's his call. My instinct is opt-in with an honest sentence, offered where the feature is, not on first launch — you don't get to burn somebody's battery to make your feature look fast.

foobar's ReplayGain scan is the precedent people know: you point at a selection and it grinds, visibly, and you can stop it. Nobody minds a long job they asked for. Everybody minds a long job they didn't.

Recorded as an open question for the owner rather than a resolution. Marcus, the shape. He was explicit: default to a blend of all the dimensions, expand to configure each, and each starts from the blend's own points.

The instruction is clear and the implementation has a trap in it. Each dimension is a rank axis — a track's position within *this* collection, nought to one. If the blend is the unweighted mean of those ranks, then loud-and-slow and quiet-and-fast both land at 0.5, and a curve drawn through the middle can be satisfied by tracks that sound nothing like each other.
Which is exactly the complaint he made in the first place — 'the dots don't follow my line'. If the mean is degenerate, he'll see a line that's satisfied and a playlist that isn't.

Two ways out, and they're both honest. One: the blend is a *weighted* mean with energy dominant — energy at roughly six-tenths, brightness and density sharing the rest — because energy is the dimension a listener actually perceives as the arc of a playlist. Two: keep the mean but add a tolerance band per dimension, so a track can only satisfy the blend if no single dimension is wildly off. I'd ship the first and hold the second in reserve.
And the label says what it does, in listener words. Not 'blend'. 'Loud, fast and busy at the top; quiet, slow and sparse at the bottom.'
That's the axis label solved, and it's better copy than anything on the page today. The word 'dimension' should never appear on screen. What Baz listens for. That's the expander's name.

On the expansion: if the blend is a weighted mean, then seeding each dimension with the blend's points is mathematically consistent — set every dimension to the same curve and the weighted mean is that curve, whatever the weights. So his instruction survives the change intact. Say that in the doc, because it's the kind of thing that gets 'simplified' later by somebody who doesn't know why it held.

My turn, and I have three, in order of how badly they'd fail somebody. First: the curve is drag-only. A control you can only operate by holding a button and moving a pointer accurately is closed to anybody with a tremor, anybody on a trackpad in a moving train, and anybody who works by keyboard. baz's own accessibility promise says every action has a visible, pointer-reachable control — this is the mirror failure and the charter doesn't currently cover it.

So the shape presets are not decoration, they are the accessible route to the same outcome, and they should be *under* the curve as first-class controls rather than a row of thumbnails above it. And the points want arrow-key nudging once selected, with visible focus.
Agreed, and I'd add hit targets. Those handles are small. In a curve editor you give the grab region twice the drawn radius, because the drawn dot is a label for a region, not the region.

Second: the pairing between a row and its dot is carried by hover and by colour. The owner is colour blind, which the project already knows and has written down. Hovering a row must do something a colour-blind person on a still screenshot can read: enlarge the dot, drop a tick to the axis, and put the position number in the row itself. Three cues, none of which is hue.
I didn't know hovering did anything at all, for what it's worth.

Third, and smallest: the curve needs a text alternative. Even without a screen reader in the toolkit, the shape can be stated in a sentence beside it — 'starts quiet, climbs to a peak two-thirds through, comes down'. It's cheap, it helps everybody, and it's the only version of the control a future accessibility tree could read.
That sentence exists in the code already, as the shape descriptions. It's just hidden behind picking a preset. Put it under the curve permanently and update it as the curve is dragged.
That's the strongest thing said so far. It turns the graphic into something you can verify without seeing it.
Can we talk about what happens *after* Compose? Because in the mockup the list is a list of names and then there's a quiet line saying save or play. That's not a playlist, that's a receipt.

The people who use this will immediately want to: remove the two tracks they hate, drag one up, keep the rest, and save it with a name they choose. If Recompose then silently throws that away, they'll do it once and never trust the feature again.

So the result pane is the ordinary playlist row set, with the ordinary controls, and Recompose is a labelled act that says what it will cost: 'Compose again — your changes to this list will be replaced.' If there are no edits, no warning.
Or Recompose adds rather than replaces? No — too clever. Replace, with a warning, and undo covers the mistake.

There's also the variation case. Same words, same shape, different draw. Every generative feature needs a 'not this, again' button or people conclude it only knows one answer. The engine already carries a variation seed.
That's the button I actually wanted. Twice.
Length. The proposal quietly dropped the length picker into the Compose button and didn't say so.
How long is it? That's the second question I asked out loud, after what do I type.

Then it belongs on the button, and in listener units. 'Compose about an hour' rather than 'Compose · 20 tracks'. Tracks are the engine's unit; time is the listener's. A drive is ninety minutes; nobody thinks in tracks.
Both, honestly. 'Compose · about an hour' and the count arrives in the result's own line once it exists. Time first.

Now let me do the job I was invited for. The page today asks for: a mood, some words, a shape, a number of extra curves, a length, and a press. That's six. My cut: mood, words, shape, press. Length folds into the press. Extra curves go behind the expander. The local-analysis block goes to Settings, where every other machine-facing readout in this product lives.

And I want the fork gone. Before any of this you must choose Manual or Vibe from a screen that exists only to ask which of two things you meant. That's the sentence in the top right the owner told you to delete — it's there to explain a fork that shouldn't exist.
Yes. One New playlist page. 'Start from a mood' at the top with the chips; 'Start with an empty list' as a quieter line underneath. Same page, same save, same file at the end.
That's better than my proposal, and it removes the offending line by removing its reason rather than by hiding it.
It also removes a whole navigation step, which is the cheapest accessibility win in the room.
Can I ask why a track is in the list? Because I looked at that curve and the dots and I still don't know why the fourth song is the fourth song.

This is the trust surface and the proposal doesn't have one. Select a row and one line appears beneath the curve: 'position 4 of 20 — louder than 78% of your library, matched *warm analogue soul*.' It answers the owner's original demand, which was that a person can see it really worked.
Say 'louder than 78% of your library' rather than any number that looks like a score. It's a rank, it's true, and it's the one framing that doesn't invite the reader to think there's a rating.
And that line is the same information the hover pairing carries, in words, which is the text alternative I asked for arriving for free.

Naming, while we're here. 'Vibe' is fine as the thing's name — it's short and people say it. But the page's own sentence should say what happens: 'Describe it, shape it, and Baz builds it from music you already own.' The current byline says 'a playlist composed from the music on this device', which is a sentence about a device.
The device thing did make me wonder if it was uploading something.

Which is precisely backwards, since the whole point is that it doesn't. The privacy line should be a plain one, once: 'Your music never leaves this computer.' Not 'your audio never leaves Baz', which sounds like a policy.

Back to layout for a moment, because there's a hole in the narrow case. In the stacked order — ask, curve, list — a listener on a 1000-pixel window scrolls past the entire form to see the result, presses Compose at the top, and then scrolls again. The proposal fixed the wide case and left the narrow one as it was.

Two ways: pin the Compose control to the foot of the ask block so it's always in reach, or switch to two tabs — Ask and List — under the breakpoint. I'd pin. Tabs hide the result behind a press, which is what we're trying to stop doing.
Pin it. And when a compose has happened, the narrow layout should land you on the list, not back at the top of the form.

One performance note so nobody designs something we can't build. Retrieval over an already-analysed library is fast — it's a shortlist per position over vectors in memory. Composing on every drag would be affordable *computationally* and is still wrong, because a result that changes under your hand can't be read. Keep Compose explicit.

But show the library's own distribution behind the curve live, which the widget already draws. That's the honest feedback during a drag: not 'here's a new playlist', but 'there is very little of your music up here'.

And when a curve asks for something the collection cannot fill — the workout shape over a library of chamber music — say so in that language. 'Your library has little above this line; Baz will get as close as it can.' Degrading silently is what makes people think the feature is broken.
That sentence is worth more than the six mood presets put together.

Section headers, briefly, because the owner's sentence reads two ways and I don't want to guess. Home and this page share one small-caps helper; Library and Playlists use the wall's band. He said he prefers 'the library and homepage'.

The two do different jobs, and that's probably what he's feeling rather than saying. The wall's band separates *runs of content*. The small-caps rule labels *parts of a form*. Using the band for form sections would be a category error dressed as consistency.

Agreed — but if the redesign lands, this page stops being a form and starts being a place with content in it, so the band becomes the right answer here anyway. The question then only really applies to Home.
Then I'll put it to him narrowly: the band on this page for certain, and Home either way — his call, one line to change.
Nobody has said anything about the six moods. Are they good moods?
They're fine. Late-night drive, Sunday morning, Focus, Workout, Wind down, Party. That's the set every product ships because it's the set that covers most evenings.
The one I'd add is the one nobody ships: 'Something I haven't played in a while'. baz has a play ledger. It knows. And it's the request people actually make of a big library.
That's not a mood, it's a filter, and it composes with all of them. I'd make it a toggle beside the words rather than a seventh chip: 'lean towards things I haven't played lately'.
I would press that every single time.
That's a new feature and it's a good one. It goes to the owner as a proposal, not into this redesign.

Two smaller things before we close. The disclosure triangle for 'what Baz listens for' needs to be a real control with a label — a bare triangle with grey text is the least discoverable widget in interface design. And whatever the empty state says when the library is unlistened must not be an error colour. It isn't an error. It's a beginning.
'Baz hasn't listened to your music yet' with a labelled button underneath, and the button says what it does: 'Listen to my library'. Not 'Start analysis'.
With the honest cost beside it, once it can be measured: roughly how long, and that it can be stopped and resumed. Which it can — the index is on disk and the workers are re-entrant.

Last thing from me. This feature is the most distinctive thing in the product and it is buried behind a fork, on a page most people will never open. When it works, it should be offered from the wall — press a record, 'more like this' — and that is where it will earn its keep. Out of scope today, but somebody should write it down.
Write it down and don't build it. One page at a time.
Let me read back what I think we've agreed, and then I'll take the disagreements separately.

Confirmed from the proposal: two panes at width; the list beside the controls; a mood press as the first move; one blended line by default with per-dimension curves behind a disclosure seeded from the blend; the strip sentence gone; chips that look pressable.

Changed by this room: the cold start is the primary state, not a footnote; the blend is a weighted mean with energy dominant, and it says so in listener words; the words get a small vocabulary chosen against the baseline corpus, not two examples; the curve gets keyboard, bigger targets, a permanent sentence describing it, and presets as its accessible route; the row-to-dot pairing carries position and a tick, never hue alone; length is on the button in minutes; the Manual/Vibe fork dies and takes the offending sentence with it; the result is an editable playlist with a warned Recompose and a variation press; a selected row explains itself in one line; the narrow layout pins Compose and lands on the list.

Open for the owner: whether baz may listen in the background before being asked, and on what consent; whether Home keeps its small-caps sections; whether 'haven't played in a while' becomes a real control; and whether this feature eventually reaches the wall as 'more like this'.
If you do the vocabulary chips and the button says how long it'll be, I'd use it.
And if Recompose eats my edits without asking, I won't.
Nothing here requires a screen reader to be honest, which is the bar this product can currently meet. Don't let the curve ship without the sentence.
And don't let the words ship without a scored run. It's the difference between a feature and a superstition.
Agreed on all three. Thank you — I'll write this up against the design note and the backlog.

title: The cold start is the page's primary state
body: A library baz has not listened to is the state most first visits are in, and the proposal treated it as a footnote. The right-hand pane becomes an honest progress reading with a partial list forming in it, the mood chips stay pressable, and no copy promises a playlist in one press until the library has been heard.

title: The blend is a weighted mean, energy dominant, named in listener words
body: An unweighted mean of rank axes is degenerate: loud-and-slow and quiet-and-fast both satisfy the middle of the line, which is the same failure the owner already reported once. Energy carries roughly six-tenths, brightness and density share the rest, and the axis is labelled 'loud, fast and busy' to 'quiet, slow and sparse'. Seeding each dimension from the blend stays exactly consistent under weighting, so the owner's instruction survives intact.

title: Words get a vocabulary, not a rule
body: Three rows of four chips — what it is made of, what it feels like, how it moves — that append to the field and teach the register in seconds. Freeform typing stays. The chips are chosen by a scored run against the baseline corpus (backlog item 59), not by taste.

title: The curve becomes operable without a mouse and readable without sight of it
body: Arrow-key nudging on a selected point with visible focus; grab regions at twice the drawn radius; the shape presets promoted to the accessible route to the same outcome; and a permanent sentence under the curve that states the shape in words and updates as it is dragged.

title: Row-to-dot pairing never rests on hue
body: Hovering or selecting a row enlarges its dot, drops a tick to the axis, and shows the position number in the row itself. Three cues, none of them a colour, which is the standing rule in this project.

title: Length lives on the commitment, in minutes
body: 'Compose · about an hour', with the track count arriving in the result's own line. Time is the listener's unit; tracks are the engine's.

title: The Manual/Vibe fork dies
body: One New playlist page: 'Start from a mood' with the chips, 'Start with an empty list' underneath. This deletes the sentence the owner asked to remove by deleting its reason, and removes a navigation step.

title: The result is a playlist, not a receipt
body: Ordinary rows with ordinary controls: reorder, remove, save under a name, play. Recompose states what it replaces when there are edits to replace, and a variation press asks the same question again for a different answer.

title: A selected row explains itself in one line
body: 'Position 4 of 20 — louder than 78% of your library, matched *warm analogue soul*.' A rank, never a score. This is the owner's original demand — that a person can see it really worked — in a form that survives a screenshot.

title: A request the library cannot fill says so
body: 'Your library has little above this line; Baz will get as close as it can', shown against the distribution the widget already draws. Silent degradation is what makes people think a feature is broken.

title: The narrow layout pins the commitment and lands on the result
body: Stacking ask, curve and list in reading order left the narrow case exactly as it was. Compose pins to the foot of the ask block, and after a compose the page shows the list rather than the top of the form.

title: Machine-facing readouts move to Settings
body: The local-analysis block belongs where every other machine-facing readout in the product already lives. One honest pool line stays on the page.

title: May baz listen to the library before it is asked to?
body: Analysis is hours of CPU on a large library and battery on a laptop. Doing it quietly at first launch makes the feature instant when found; not doing it makes the first use slow. The room would not decide this: it is a consent question and it is the owner's.
provenance: Lena raised it; Sam and Ines argued for opt-in with an honest cost, on the feature's own page rather than at launch.

title: Does Home keep its small-caps section headers?
body: The band belongs on this page once it stops being a form. Home is the genuinely ambiguous half of the owner's sentence, and it is one line to change either way.
provenance: Jonas argued the two treatments do different jobs; Priya noted the argument dissolves here once the page becomes a place.

title: Does 'something I haven't played in a while' become a control?
body: baz keeps a play ledger, so it can answer this, and it is the request people actually make of a large library. Proposed as a toggle beside the words rather than a seventh mood.
provenance: Ines proposed it; Marcus reframed it as a filter that composes with every mood; Toby said he would press it every time.

title: Does this eventually reach the wall as 'more like this'?
body: The most distinctive thing in the product is currently behind a fork on a page most people will never open. Out of scope for this phase, recorded so it is not lost.
provenance: Ines raised it; Sam agreed to write it down and not build it.
